vignette:
**Vignette: Dr. Meena R., Age 80**

Meena has practiced dentistry for over fifty years, and even now, at eighty, she keeps three half-days a week at the small clinic she built from nothing in the early 1970s. Her hands still steady when she works. It is the only place, she says quietly, where she feels entirely like herself.

Four years ago, Meena was visiting her younger sister in a city she had known since childhood. They were in a crowded market on a Tuesday morning — the kind of market she had walked through as a girl, full of marigolds and the smell of frying bread — when a bomb detonated two stalls away. The blast threw her against a concrete pillar. Her sister was injured badly enough to require surgery. Three other people nearby did not survive. Meena was physically unharmed in any way that showed on an X-ray. She flew home ten days later, once her sister was stable, and she has not returned since.

For the first several months, she told herself she was simply tired. She is eighty years old, after all, and she had been through a divorce decades ago, raised two children largely alone, built a career in a country that did not always welcome her. She knows something about endurance. But the tiredness did not lift, and it was not ordinary tiredness. It was something heavier — a constant low-grade vigilance that followed her from room to room in her flat.

She began noticing sounds differently. The pneumatic drill in her own surgery — a sound she has lived alongside for half a century — sometimes catches her without warning and sends a cold wave through her chest that she cannot immediately explain. She sets down her instruments and breathes until it passes. Her nurse has noticed, though neither of them has spoken of it directly.

At night, Meena wakes between two and four in the morning. She lies in the dark and the market comes back to her — not always the blast itself, but the moment just before it: the light through the canvas awnings, a child's red sandal on the ground, the particular quality of the noise the crowd made. She replays that sequence and cannot find the place where she might have changed what happened. She knows, rationally, that there is no such place. This does not help.

She has become careful about where she goes. She avoids the shopping centre near her clinic now, particularly on weekends when it is full. She takes a longer route to avoid the bus station. She tells herself this is practical, that she is simply an old woman being sensible about crowds. But she recognizes, in the honest part of herself, that she is frightened in a way she was not before, and that the fear has quietly rearranged her life without her fully consenting to it.

What troubles her most, she says, is what has happened to her relationship with her sister. They speak on the phone every Sunday, as they always have, but something has shifted. Meena finds herself unable to ask too many questions about how her sister is recovering, because the answers pull her back into the market, and she cannot afford to go there in the middle of an ordinary Sunday. She feels the distance between them and does not know how to close it without opening something she is not sure she can manage.

She carries all of this with the same composure she brings to her patients — the warm efficiency, the steady hands, the way she explains each procedure before she begins so no one is frightened. Her colleagues see a woman who has simply slowed down a little, gracefully, as one does at eighty. What they do not see is that she arrives twenty minutes early each morning and sits in her car in the car park, preparing herself to walk through the door.
